rows.b: A radiation-hardened computer that flies the spacecraft, aims the antennas, and runs the science instruments. It must work for years with no repair shop.
Alternating atomic layers of different semiconductors create artificial crystals with engineered electronic properties. They make precise lasers and detectors.
His original plane: a vast grid of cells following his own rule-set, growing patterns that compute. Programs are starting patterns; answers are the shapes the grid settles into.
His original engine: a cascade of deterministic stages where the same input always gives the same output, down to the last bit. It proves its answers by replaying them, step for step, on demand.
His original system architecture: processor, memory, and interconnect woven into one deterministic fabric where every signal's path is known in advance. Nothing is left to chance, ever.
His original arithmetic unit: an ALU that encodes numbers in golden-ratio base, where multiplication by phi is just a shift. It finds the elegant path through every calculation.
His original memory: storage cells folded into hexagonal prisms, packing more bits per area than square grids. Each hex cell knows its six neighbors, so data can flow in any direction.

His original fusion processor: eleven computing lenses — deterministic, probabilistic, geometric, hash, neural, evolutionary, fuzzy, swarm, decision-tree, cellular, and hybrid fusion — on one chip, voting on every answer.

His original machine: a three-dimensional lattice of tiny switches where data flows along crystal paths instead of wires. Every layer of the lattice is both memory and processor, so nothing ever travels far.
His original AI machine: neural networks are woven on a loom-like frame where each thread is a connection with an adjustable weight. Training is literally re-weaving, visible to the eye.

His original processor core: every instruction is checked by a twin circuit before it runs, so paradoxes and contradictions are caught and resolved, never executed. It is the hardware heart of his paradox-immune system.
His original unit: a probabilistic engine that collapses chance into certainty by running every branch deterministically and keeping the proven winner. Randomness in, proof out.
His original quantum design: qubits are threads on a loom, and quantum gates are the shuttle weaving them into entangled fabric. The pattern of the weave IS the program, readable at a glance.
His original array: thousands of tiny simple gates that vote on every decision like a swarm, so no single failure can corrupt an answer. The swarm re-routes around dead gates automatically.
His original registers: a stack where every value carries its own timestamp, so the processor can reach back to any past state without saving snapshots. Time travel for data, built in.
A hard crystal that switches high voltages and shrugs off heat that would kill silicon. It drives electric cars and solar inverters efficiently.
Purified sand becomes the crystal wafer on which billions of transistors are printed. Complementary pairs of transistors switch with almost no wasted power.
Light guides etched into silicon carry data as photons instead of electrons, moving information faster with less heat. It already links datacenters; logic is next.
Single electrons trapped in tiny silicon dots use their spin as a qubit. Because they are made with chip-factory methods, they could one day sit beside regular transistors.
A complete computer on one small board with ports for screen, USB, and electronics projects. It runs a full operating system from a memory card.
A memory where each bit is a single switchable molecule, reaching densities no lithography can touch. SPECULATION: stable arrays do not exist yet.
A future device where tiny magnetic whirlpools race along tracks, storing and processing data as they move. SPECULATION: controlled skyrmion circuits are still research.
A complete computer on the wrist that tracks health, shows messages, and runs apps on a tiny efficient chip. It charges rarely and works all day.
Memory cells that store bits in the magnetic direction of electron spins, keeping data with no power. It is fast like RAM and permanent like a disk.
Thousands of computers linked by fast networks act as one machine for weather, physics, and AI. Each node is ordinary; the teamwork is extraordinary.
Logic built from superconducting loops that pass single quantum pulses of magnetic flux, switching hundreds of times faster than silicon while barely warming.
Qubits made of superconducting circuits chilled near absolute zero, controlled by microwave pulses. They run quantum algorithms that no regular computer can simulate at scale.
